text: Half a century before that phone call, Casey was a lanky 14-year-old chasing another boy through the streets of Bucktoosh.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey had gone home, recovered overnight, and returned the next morning to even the score.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: When a teacher interrupted the rematch, Casey began throwing stones at her.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: His father's judgment was swift.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey would leave Bucktoosh and live 60 miles north in Millerton with his older half-sister Jen and her husband, a minister.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: His father, James Durgavel Irving, known simply as JD, owned the sawmill that processed many of these trees.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The mill supplied the wages, and the store recovered some of those wages.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: J.D.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The housekeeper he eventually hired, Mary Elizabeth Gifford, was a young orphan who had taught herself bookkeeping, and in time he married her.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: On March 14, 1899, Mary gave birth to a son.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: They named him Kenneth Colin Irving.

text: Most would simply call him K.C.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Mary adored him, and he adored her right back.

speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: They counted his earnings and placed them inside a large clock in the dining room.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Properly washed, he discovered these bottles could be sold for a neat profit.

text: Before long, two older boys were working for him.

text: He owned the pull cart and he ran the show.

text: He applied that judgment to others, but to no one harder than himself.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And it wasn't long after that he quit the violin that the fighting started.

text: Sailors drank at the town's hotels and then battled it out on the streets.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Being good with your fists was a mark of distinction.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: One Irving employee recalled stopping his horse to watch young Casey scrap.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He'd urge him on and then hoist the battered boy up onto the wagon and preach to him about his behavior.

text: The preaching didn't take.

text: You had a certain amount of energy, Casey explained later.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: You had to get rid of it somehow.

text: By his own count, he won about half of his fights.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: But the fight that ended with him throwing stones at a teacher was one too many, and his father had finally had enough.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: On the first morning at his new school, the principal called him to his feet before the class.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Kenneth, stand up.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: You've come to learn.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: I'm going to teach you.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: I'm the boss.

text: If you fight for one minute, it's going to be too bad for you.

text: The principal quizzed him and discovered that the new boy was far behind his classmates.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He was assigned extra lessons.

text: So at night, Jen's husband tutored him by the light of a kerosene lamp.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And slowly, something began to change.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Jen, who had never liked how transfixed he had been by money, quietly went to work on him too.

text: I doubt that he earned a penny that year, she later recalled.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: By gosh, Casey remembered I got to like school.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: 70 years later, by then one of the richest men alive and the top entrepreneurs the world had ever seen, Casey called that year without earnings probably the best thing that ever happened to me.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: When Casey returned to Bucktouch, World War I had begun.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He wanted to enlist.

text: And once again, what Casey wanted would put him at odds with his father.

speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: While Casey had been away, two unlikely forces had begun to undermine Bucktouch's economy, a caterpillar and a catalog.

text: Across the county, mills had begun to shut down.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: JD's was on borrowed time.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: As usable timber dwindled, workers lost hours and wages.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: A town that had lived by cutting trees had no easy answer when the forest could no longer feed its mills.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: That wasn't the only threat he faced.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The Eaton's catalog offered rural Canadians hundreds of pages of clothing, furniture, tools, equipment, and household goods at prices a village merchant struggled with.

text: However, for JD, it threatened the survival of his general store.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: By the time Casey's summer of leisure ended, there was plenty of work waiting for him.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey's business education began behind the counter of his father's general store.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The store bought and sold whatever nearby farms grew, and in the fall that meant potatoes.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: With his father away, Casey began buying from an excellent harvest.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Get rid of them.

text: Desperate to get rid of them, Casey fired off a flurry of telegrams to buyers down the American East Coast.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: American demand seemed inexhaustible, so he raised his prices.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Soon he was shipping nearly the whole stock to New York City at $18 a barrel, considerably more than he had paid for it.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: More than a year passed before he learned the reason for his good fortune.

text: While luck had rescued his potato gamble, the next opportunity he seized came from foresight.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Automobiles were beginning to appear more frequently on the dirt roads.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: To many people, they are a rich man's toy, but Casey saw opportunity.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The Eaton's catalog, like this year's catalog, could sell a farmer almost anything his father's store did that wasn't perishable.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: A farmer who owned a car had to buy that locally.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: So without permission, Casey signed up his father's store as an agent for Imperial Oil, then Canada's largest oil company.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: At six o'clock one summer morning in 1920, while the village slept, he was outside the store digging a hole for a 250-gallon gasoline tank.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: When his father asked what he was doing, Casey answered over a shovel, I'm darn sure we're not going out of business.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The problem with selling gasoline is that there were still too few customers.

text: To Casey, the solution was obvious.

text: He would sell cars.

text: He signed a deal with the Ford Motor Company to become his county's official car dealer.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Ford supplied the cars and Casey earned a commission on each one he sold.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Soon he was on the road every day of the week, intent on putting a car in every farmyard in the county.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Each morning, dressed in a suit and freshly shined shoes, he knocked on farmhouse doors and tried to persuade men who had spent their entire lives behind horses to buy a machine that they had never owned before.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: His father thought the whole endeavor would be the ruination of the countryside.

text: So Casey accepted whatever they could offer.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: His responsibility did not stop with a sale either.

speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: You had to have happy customers, he said.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: You didn't leave people in a lot of trouble.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: One morning, a local storekeeper named William Graham had a truck that wouldn't start.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: So Casey came over and got it running.

text: Casey made about $105 on every Ford that he sold.

text: The following year, he made $22,000, which works out to roughly $350,000 today.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: It was an extraordinary income for a man in his 20s operating out of a small village.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: When Casey later spoke fondly about those years, it was the people he remembered, though, not the money.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: I never enjoyed anything more than talking to those farmers, he said.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: At this point, Casey was selling the cars, servicing them, and supplying the gasoline that kept them moving.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: But the gas belonged to Imperial Oil, and they were about to remind him of that.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey's car sales were booming when a neighbor arrived with bad news.

text: Imperial Oil had quietly purchased a lot in town and hired its own full-time agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The company was preparing to cut him off without warning.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The explanation when he finally got one was simple.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The area's other merchants had complained to Imperial that the only place to buy gasoline was from the Irving store, which competed with them and everything else.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Cayce was angry, but he understood the business logic, saying later, from Imperial's standpoint, the move made sense, but he might have told me what he was going to do.

speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The company was controlled by the Standard Oil Empire, and they were not fond of competition.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: They expected him to stick to selling cars.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Instead, he went looking for a new supply of gasoline.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He found one in Tulsa, Oklahoma, nearly 2,000 miles away.

text: He wired the money south and arranged for the gasoline to be shipped north in a railway tank car.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Solving that problem created another.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: When the gas arrived, Casey needed somewhere to store it, so he ordered a 10,000-gallon tank, 40 times the size of the one he'd buried a few years earlier.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: In Bakhtouche, the neighbors were soon saying Casey Irving would be skinned alive by the giant Imperial oil.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The battle between them became visible in a very unexpected way.

speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: After his tank was installed, a fire marshal informed Casey that it stood too close to the surrounding buildings, and so he had to move the entire thing and begin again.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Once the tank was finally in place, he built a garage and service station across from the family store.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He invited his father and half-brother to join the venture.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Both declined, presumably because they thought, too, that Imperial Oil would quickly put them out of business.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: All right, Casey said, I'll do it alone.

text: And that was no accident.

text: Casey had positioned it where motorists could see it from as far down the road as possible.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The same emphasis on roadside visibility would eventually become a hallmark of the Irving oil stations, with their broad canopies appearing across the region.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: But visibility would not be enough.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: To compete with Imperial, Casey knew that he had to have a better product.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: So he took his Tulsa gasoline and blended his own recipe, one that could fire faster in cold engines.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And then he pitched that to every farmer who had ever cursed while cranking their engine on a freezing January morning.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He even outnamed the competition.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He gave it a name that challenged his competitors directly.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Before long, he was doing 95% of the gasoline business in Bucktoosh.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: By 1925, Casey Irving had another problem.

text: Ford told Casey to stay in his own territory.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: But Casey did not like being told what to do.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: It's open territory, he said.

text: By the time World War II began, Casey was 40 years old.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: On his desk sat radio equipment that could connect him to employees across all of his operations.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: When someone asked whether he really had to oversee everything himself, Casey said, you do if you want to stay in business.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: When asked why he delegated so little, because I can't stand to see other people make mistakes.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: His employees put it this way, when your boss knows more about your job than you do, it keeps you on your toes.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: One of his biographers later wrote that New Brunswick was a province where all the things Kenneth Cole Irving did were judged to be more remarkable because they happened here, and until he did them, no one thought they could be done.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: In 1939, the remarkable things were just beginning.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: His still small oil company was standing up to the giants.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: His shipping business existed out of spite for a government railway.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: His buses were built by sawing automobiles apart and thousands of acres of forest had somehow survived the budworm and the depression.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Then on September 1st, Germany invaded Poland and the world went to war for the second time in his life.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The first war he had missed, and this one would make him.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The first part of Casey Irving's business to be transformed by the war was a small veneer company he had purchased the year before.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Canada Veneers had been started by a group of St. John businessmen in 1933.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: It made veneer, which is wood-shaped into sheets thinner than cardboard, which it turned mostly into orange crates.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: By 1938, the company was struggling and Casey had stepped in and took control.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He bought it because it was cheap and he thought he could fix it.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The war changed the company's fortunes overnight.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: In England, the aircraft company de Havilland was designing a bomber made largely of wood.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Metal was already scarce, and the war was making it even scarcer.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The plane was called the Mosquito, and it was built almost entirely from plywood.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Thin sheets of veneer stacked and glued together until the wood became both light and remarkably strong.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The crews called it the wooden wonder.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: For a good stretch of the war, it was about the fastest thing in the sky.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: It could fly from Britain to Berlin, photograph targets or drop bombs, and get home untouched.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Yellow birch was especially well suited to making plywood for the plane, and New Brunswick had it in abundance, and Cayce already owned a plant that could turn it into veneer.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: So when Britain called for every sheet of aircraft plywood the empire could produce, Canada veneers suddenly found itself making something the war badly needed.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The little plant that had nearly gone out of business in 1938 was soon running seven days a week, with 500 people working around the clock.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: More than 6,000 mosquitoes were eventually built, riding on the sheets of wood like those coming out of Casey's plants.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey never pretended he had seen any of this coming.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Too many successful business people clean up the story afterwards until eventually every lucky break looked like foresight.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey didn't do that with Canada Veneers.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He had bought a broken company because it was cheap and he thought he could fix it.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Then the war came and saved it.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: But the war work pouring into Canada Veneers was not reaching much of the rest in New Brunswick.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Most of Canada's big wartime factories were going to Ontario and Quebec, where most of the country's people and their votes were.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The maritime provinces had fewer of both and much less war work was coming their way.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: So Casey went to the nation's capital, Ottawa, to ask for some for his province.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He was turned away.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: So he went back, he was turned away again, and he kept going back until he finally came home with a contract to build invasion supply barges.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey put the work in Bucktoosh, his hometown.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He built bunkhouses on the old family farm for the workers to sleep in.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: His shipyards would eventually turn out more than a thousand barges.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And after D-Day, many of them carried supplies that kept the invasion moving.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The Warriors handed him his next deal, too.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: In 1942, a bankrupt pulp company in upstate New York owed Casey Irving some money.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The company was Dexter Sulfite.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Its debt had ended up in the hands of a United States federal agency, which was now trying to sell the business.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Several companies were interested, and most of them were offering around 10 cents on the dollar.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey offered something very different.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He would pay the full amount with interest.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: There was, however, one condition.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He wanted four years to do it, which only made sense if he could take the broken pulp company and get it earning money again.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Those earnings could then pay for the company.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: To the government employees reviewing his bids, that sounded naive.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: At one point, an official pulled Dexter's lawyer aside and asked him, where did you find that huckleberry?
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: When the remark got back to Casey, he was puzzled.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: A huckleberry?
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Why did he call me a huckleberry?
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: A Huckleberry meant a country bumpkin, someone foolish enough in the official's eyes to pay full price when everyone else was offering much less.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: It was meant as an insult, but Casey adopted the nickname with delight.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He saw himself as the underdog.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He took over at Dexter in May of 1942, put more than 600 people to work, and paid the mortgage off with interest before the four years were up.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: One of the people who helped this remarkable turnaround was Frank Lang, an Austrian-born engineer who soon became one of Dexter's key operators.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey's verdict on Lang was simple.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He knew what I didn't, and vice versa.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And Lang told a story about his new boss that I think is particularly indicative of Irving.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: There was a serious problem at the mill one day.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Serious enough that Lang wanted permission to shut the whole operation down while they found the cause.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey listened and then asked about one particular valve.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Had someone checked it?
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Lang insisted it had been checked.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey asked again, gently, Mr. Lang, I wonder if you would check that valve?
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Lang did, and it turned out Casey was right.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Fixing it avoided the shutdown entirely.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: That was the strange thing about Casey Irving.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: His businesses stretched across industries and countries, but his attention could still zero in on a single valve.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: If you're wondering why a man who was already successful would buy a dying mill in another country and spend years turning it around, you weren't alone.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: People would ask Casey Irving some version of that question for the rest of his life.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: His answer had very little to do with money.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: I like to see wheels turning, he said.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Years later, he put it another way.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: I've always enjoyed what I did.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: If you're busy, you get interested.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: It's like the fiddler at the dance.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: You'd almost play for nothing.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: As the war increased the demand for veneer and lumber, Casey began buying Timberland on a scale he never had before.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He needed yellow birch for Canada veneers and lumber for the barges, and by now his instinct was familiar.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: If raw material mattered enough to the business, he would rather own the source than depend on somebody else for it.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The biggest opportunity came with a defunct railway that still owned nearly 700,000 acres of forest, an area almost the size of Rhode Island.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Before Casey bought it, he needed to know what was actually there.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He could have hired a timber expert, read the report, and made his decision from the office.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Instead, he hired an expert and put on his snowshoes and went into the woods with him.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: For days, they walked through the property counting trees.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: At night, back at camp, Casey compared his count with the inspectors.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: If the numbers disagreed, they went back into the woods and counted again.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Only when the two counts matched was Casey satisfied enough to write the check.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: While Casey used experts, managers, accountants, and reports throughout his businesses, he refused to outsource his own judgment.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He wanted to see and understand things for himself.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The same habit brought him to his companies after dark, often without warning to walk through them himself.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Night visits, he said, are the best way to find out what's going on.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: His rule was simple.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: If you know both ends and the middle of a business, you should be able to make the right decisions.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: That was his advantage.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He knew the business from A to Z.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: While Casey's businesses expanded through the Depression and the war, his three sons were growing up.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Home was a big white house on Mount Pleasant Avenue, and from its upstairs window, you could watch the Irving ships come into the harbor.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The house ran on the patience of Casey's wife, Harriet.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Late at night, with her husband still bent over the papers downstairs, she would call down from the bedroom.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Kenneth, it's after 11.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: No answer but the scratching of his pen.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: An hour later, she would try again.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Kenneth, it's midnight.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: All right, honey, Casey would answer.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: I'll be up shortly.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: She occasionally joined Casey on his night visits and waited in the car while he disappeared inside a mill.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: One night, a worker stepped outside for some errand found her sitting alone, knitting.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Harriet rolled down the window and asked if he had seen her husband.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Yes, the man said Mr. Irving was still inside.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: What would he mind telling Kenneth that she thought it was about time he came home?
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: That was Hattie.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The fortune changed almost everything around her without changing her very much.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The same thing could be said for KC.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: She still gave friends homemade jams and preserves for Christmas, and when someone called her Miss Irving, she corrected them.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: I'm Hattie.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: A friend who had known her before the money said it best.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: She was no different from when she worked in the store in Bucktoosh.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey and Hattie had three sons, Jim, Arthur, and Jack.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And by the end of the war, the Boers were growing up in one of the wealthiest families in New Brunswick, if not the country.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And Casey understood the problem this created.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Making money had taken him most of his life.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: His sons were going to receive the benefits of it simply by being born.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He could leave them a fortune, but the harder job was making sure the fortune didn't make them helpless or spoiled.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Their business education began with 12 hens.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The boys called their operation the Jim, Art, and Jack Farm.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: They sold the eggs, kept the books, and advertised around the neighborhood.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: It was a tiny business, but Casey treated it as seriously as he treated all of his other businesses.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And the boys quickly learned that customers could teach them lessons that their father could not.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: When they eventually sold some of their hens, the buyer loaded the birds into his van and then counted out less money than he had agreed to pay.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He was already preparing to leave when 12-year-old Jim climbed into the van and announced that nobody was going anywhere until the rest of the money appeared.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The man paid up.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Jim remembered the lesson for the rest of his life.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Never do business with someone who's in such a hurry that he has the ignition on and his foot on the accelerator.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Of course, Casey offered lessons of his own.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: One New Year's Eve, Jim came home from celebrating and went straight to bed.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: At half past midnight, his father woke him up.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Dad woke me up and I thought he was going to wish me a Happy New Year, Jim remarked.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Instead, Casey wanted to know why there were eggs sitting on the kitchen table.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Jim had forgotten to make his deliveries.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He spent his first hour of the new year delivering eggs.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: As the boys grew older, their education moved from the chicken coop into the larger family businesses.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: None of the three finished university.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Arthur left because he believed he would learn more working beside his father.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Jim came home at 19 and told Casey he had quit as well.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: His father's response was simple, get to work.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And all of them did.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Jim gravitated towards the forest and mills, and Arthur became one of Irving's oil's strongest salesmen.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And Jack began on construction crews and stayed close to that side of the business.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: They were not simply waiting to inherit their father's companies.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: They were learning the different pieces from the inside out.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: By the 1950s, outsiders had begun to notice what Casey had built.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: A group of Montreal investors came to New Brunswick interested in buying Irving oil.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And Casey met with them for lunch and listened to their proposal.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: But he wasn't interested.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: I have three sons, he told them, and I want to keep this business for them.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: By 1948, Casey Irving had become difficult to ignore and strangely difficult to see.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: That February, Canadian business put him on the cover and guessed his fortune at about $100 million.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The cover was a sketch rather than a photograph because photographs of Casey were surprisingly hard to come by.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: A Montreal reporter who came looking for the man behind the number found Casey friendly enough, even talkative, but asked him about the inner workings of his company and very little came back.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: What he told me about himself, the reporter complained afterwards, I could have put on the back of a postage stamp.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: There was another side to that $100 million estimate.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: In a province as poor as New Brunswick, a fortune that large rested on thousands of paychecks.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And by 1948, paychecks had become one of the great arguments of the age.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: To understand what happens next, you need two pieces of context.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: First, a wave of strikes was rolling across North America.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: During the war, factories had run around the clock while wages were held down.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: When the war ended, workers across North America began demanding a larger share of the prosperity they had helped create.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Unions were winning contracts in auto plants and steel mills, and the movement had begun reaching Casey's companies too.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Second, New Brunswick presented a particular problem for workers.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: There were usually more people looking for jobs than there were jobs available.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: That gave employers leverage.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey did not need to pay what a factory in Detroit paid when there was often another man outside the gate willing to take the job at the New Brunswick rate.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: At one Irving Oil Depot, about 40 laborers formed a union.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: They were working six days and more than 50 hours a week for roughly $30.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: They wanted shorter hours, more money, and real overtime.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Bargaining dragged on for eight months.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Eventually, the union set a strike deadline.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey called the men together and told them exactly where he stood.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Anyone who failed to report for work the next morning would be fired.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The next morning, the picket line went up.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Late afternoon, a car pulled up and Casey stepped out.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: At this point, he's 49 years old and probably the richest man in New Brunswick and perhaps in the country.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And he walked over to the men who were striking against him, took off his coat and offered to settle the disagreement with his fists.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The president of the local union stood 6'4", and he looked down at Casey and grinned.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Nobody swam, and eventually Casey put his coat back on and left.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He later reduced the whole encounter to a single rule.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: It never pays to talk with your coat on.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And of the 6'4 union president, he was equally candid.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He could have made mincemeat of me.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The following morning, one of Casey's executives tried to drive through the picket line and was turned back.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: That afternoon, Casey returned, this time with company officials, policemen, and three loaded oil trucks.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The picketers allowed the cars through, but the driver of the first truck stopped.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The man standing in front of him were his own workmates, and he would not drive the truck through them.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: So Casey climbed into the cab and drove the truck through himself.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: There is something unmistakably Casey Irving about this whole situation.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The driver wouldn't do it, so the owner did.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: It was the same quality we have seen over and over again.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: When something stood between Casey and something he believed needed to be done, his instinct was to move toward the problem himself.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: That quality had helped build the empire, but at this moment, it took a different form.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Behind Casey's truck, union members claimed that a company car struck several picketers and failed to stop.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: One man ended up in the hospital.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The police did nothing.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: A few days later, a sheriff arrived with an injunction that prohibited picketing for 30 days, and this strike was effectively over.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey had won.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: But notice what happened here.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The same determination that had helped Casey stand up to the oil companies, railways, and banks was now directed at 40 of his own employees.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: They were earning roughly $30 for more than 50 hours of a workweek.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: A foreman who had worked for Casey since 1928 offered a simple explanation.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: I don't think Casey Irving likes anyone to tell him what to do.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: It would be easy to conclude that Casey Irving was simply anti-union, except he wasn't.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Two years before the oil strike, Casey had taken over a worn-out pulp mill whose previous owner had refused to allow a union at all.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Soon after the takeover, an employee showed up alone with a complaint.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey's new manager asked where the union committee was.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: There wasn't one.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The previous owner had forbidden it.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Then get one, the manager said, and a union formed within weeks.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Its first contract raised wages 19 cents an hour, and its president later said it's the best thing that ever happened when Irving got the mill.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Not long after the oil strike, leaders of the city bus union were summoned to Casey's office expecting another battle.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Instead, Casey accepted their union and they sued and received the biggest raise of their working lives.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey wasn't asking whether unions were good or bad in the abstract.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He was asking what they meant for the business in front of him.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: You could sum it up like this.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey Irving wasn't anti-union, he was pro-Irving.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And as he usually did, Casey learned from the fight, and the coat never came off again.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Fifteen years later, in 1963, workers at the Irving refinery went on strike.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: This time, Casey stayed away from the gates.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: But he did pull clerks, bookkeepers, cooks, and employees from elsewhere in the organization into the refinery and kept the plant running with roughly half its normal workforce.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The strike lasted into the following spring and ended on terms close to what Casey had offered at the very beginning.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: By the end of the war, Irving Oil had grown beyond the point where Casey could personally win every account.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The company was spreading across the Maritimes, one station and dealer at a time.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Some stations belonged to Irving Oil, but many more belonged to independent owners and merchants who agreed to sell Irving gasoline.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: By the 1950s, Irving owned roughly 300 stations and supplied another 700 dealers.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: That created a new problem.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey had built the company through his own energy and persistence, but there was only one of him.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: If Irving Oil was going to keep growing, he needed people who would pursue accounts with the same intensity he did.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: One of the best of this was Harrison McCain.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: We did an Outliers episode on Harrison, and we'll link to it in the show notes.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: McCain was young, ambitious, and already known to Casey's sons, who told their father he was one hell of a salesman.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey offered him a job, and McCain named his price.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Give me 10,000 bucks and a big car and I'm your man.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey gave him both.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: McCain noticed that Casey rarely gave direct orders to his senior people.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Instead, he would mention over lunch that a certain account would fit in just exactly.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: with Irving's plans for an area.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: McCain understood the translation.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Get your ass out there and get the account.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey told you what mattered and kind of left you to figure out how to get it done.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: McCain hadn't.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey trusted you to play your own instrument, but he expected you to play to the tempo he was setting.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: They both intended to change that, but they had very different ideas about who should do the changing.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey built with businesses.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He borrowed money, put his own capital at risk, and expected the agreements behind those investments to hold.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Robichaux, on the other hand, built with laws and taxes and public institutions.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He had been elected to serve the whole province, including counties that could not afford the services available in wealthier places.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Each man had something real to kind of point to.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: In wealthier parts of New Brunswick, local governments collected taxes from industry and spent roughly twice as much on each student as poorer areas could.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The same inequality appeared in hospitals, roads, and other public services.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Robichaud called his solution equal opportunity.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: A child in a poor country, he argued, should have the same quality of teachers and hospitals as a child in a rich one.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: To accomplish that, he needed to rebuild the province's tax system, and that brought him directly into conflict with Casey.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Robichaud saw a system tilted towards municipalities that were already rich enough to attract industry.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: But perhaps more importantly, he saw one generation of politicians signing agreements that prevented the next generation from governing freely.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And Casey saw something else entirely.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: When a town asked him to build a mill or a refinery to create jobs, he was risking millions of his own money.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: In return, they would promise certain costs would remain fixed for a period of time.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And without these concessions, the investments often wouldn't make sense.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey had put down the money, hired the workers, and kept his part of the bargain.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Now, after the money was in the ground, the government wanted to change the terms.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: To Robichaux, the agreements were privileges created by politicians who were no longer in office.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And to Casey, there were contracts.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Buried inside the equal opportunity legislation was a proposal allowing the government to cancel the old industrial agreements without compensation.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And while the proposal did not mention Casey Irving by name, it didn't need to.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: No businessman in the province had invested more in the strength of those agreements, and no businessman stood to lose more if they disappeared.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: That was why Casey had come to the legislature.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: When his turn arrived, he stood and called the proposal a breach of faith.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The government, he said, was claiming a power morally wrong, if not illegally seized.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Then he warned the politicians sitting before him, Gentlemen, you cannot get blood out of a stone, nor can you find food in an empty cupboard.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: A young opposition member watched Casey take possession of the room.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The committee was stunned, he later recalled.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: This legendary figure overwhelmed us.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Within days, the government promised to honor the existing agreements.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey had won the immediate argument.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Robichaux, nevertheless, carried equal opportunity forward and tried to transform the province's schools, hospitals, and tax system.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: But there are victories that end fights and victories that begin them.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And this was a victory that began a much larger fight.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Robichaux had watched one businessman become powerful enough to make an elected government blink.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey had witnessed a government come within inches of rewriting a bargain after his money was already in the ground.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Each man emerged from the confrontation confirming their darkest suspicions of the other.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Robichaux wondered whether Casey Irving had accumulated more power than any private citizen should possess, and Casey wondered whether a government that could discard yesterday's promises could ever be trusted with tomorrow's investments.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Five years earlier, the two builders had stood together at the refinery.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Now they had fought over the promises that helped get it built.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And the next time a Rubishow government arrived with a grand industrial plan, Casey was in no mood to trust it.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The fight over industrial development had begun before the confrontation in the legislature.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: In 1964, the government announced plans for an industrial complex at Dorchester Cape, northeast of St. John.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The centerpiece would be a new fertilizer plant.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Around it, the government imagined other factories arriving, thousands of people going to work in an overlooked part of New Brunswick entering the industrial age.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: It was precisely the sort of grand project that both Casey and Robichaux claimed to want.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: But Casey thought it was a terrible idea.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The province was already supporting another large fertilizer plant that didn't have enough demand to sustain it.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Now they found themselves proposing to build another one.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And the location was chosen more for politics than economic viability.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey's ships had worked the Bay of Fundy for years.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He knew that silt carried by the nearby rivers would settle in the shipping channel, gradually filling it.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Keeping the channel open would mean dredging it constantly.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: At one meeting, a young government official presented the projections, the plant he said would make millions of dollars almost immediately.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And Casey asked him whether that was before or after depreciation.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Before or after what?
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The official replied.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Depreciation.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: You know what depreciation is, don't you?
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The young man assured him that he did.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: So Casey asked this question again.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Were the projected profits before or after accounting for the cost of wearing out and eventually replacing the plant that produced them?
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: There was a pause.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: I'm not sure, the official admitted.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: I don't think I checked on that.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Well, thank you for that information, Casey said.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Tells me a lot.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: It was a small exchange, but it was indicative of the tension then and now between business and government.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: For Robichaux's government, the project promised jobs in a part of the province that badly needed them.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey, on the other hand, wanted to know whether it could keep paying those workers once the construction money had been spent.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey took his objections directly to Robichaux.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The meeting did not go well.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey Litter said the premier gave him the gosh-darnest lecture you ever heard.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Robichaux became in Casey's telling mad as a porcupine.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: His face turned red and he slammed his hand on the table.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Robichaux denied that version of the meeting, but there was no disagreement about the decision.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The plant was going ahead.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: As tugs nudged the first cargo ship into place, it scraped the bottom slightly.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The captain refused to tie up, and the very harbor problem that Casey had warned about was now real.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: By then, the disagreement between Casey and Robichaux had grown far beyond the fertilizer plant.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The premier and the industrialists had become symbols of two competing sources of power.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: One of Robichaux's advisors reportedly told supporters, we're going to get that bastard Irving.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Robichaux called an election and carried the feud into the campaign.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He didn't use Casey's name.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He didn't have to.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: If there is a man who wants to run this province, Robichaux declared at one rally, let him present himself to the people.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Then he carried the challenge into Bakhtush, the village where Casey had been born.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: This man who has a home not far from here, Robichaux told the crowd, this man who wants to run the province.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey Irving stayed silent.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: His son, Arthur, openly supported the opposition, and Irving Money entered the fight.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: A family that had supported the liberals for generation had turned conservative.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Then there were the newspapers.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey owned most of them, and while he insisted that he had never told the editors what to print, his critics would argue that an editor did not need instructions from the man who signed the checks.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: That argument was coming, but not just yet.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: For a moment, Robichaux was asking voters who should govern New Brunswick, the man who owned so much of it, or the people they elected to represent him.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: When the votes were counted, Robichaux's liberals won.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: But elections didn't revive the plant.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: In October 1968, it closed.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The project was meant to revive that region had left the government counting heavy losses.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Years later, Robichaux conceded the point.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: In the final analysis, he said Casey Irving was right.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: It was a failure.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey's warnings had been vindicated, but his family had backed the losing side, and Robichaux had kept his government.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And the fertilizer plant was only one of their many disputes.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: At another project, Casey had millions of dollars and his own money tied up in a hole in the ground.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The hole was in the hills of northern New Brunswick.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: It was part of the Brunswick mining project built around one of the largest deposits of lead and zinc ever found in the region.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The ore was incredibly valuable, but the lead and zinc were tangled so finely through the rock that processing it was difficult.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The question was whether the smelter they planned to build could do it at a profit.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Louis Robichaux had promised the people of northern New Brunswick that the deposit would be developed.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He argued the mine would create jobs and the smelter would create an entire industry.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And for a region desperate for hope, the project carried the promise of something larger than profit.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: In 1961, before the two had become enemies, Robichaux had sent the prospector behind the discovery, James Boylan, to see Casey Irving.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey heard him out and agreed to put millions of dollars into the project.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: His involvement helped raise millions more, and Irving's engineering company took on much of the construction, while other Irving companies supplied the materials, equipment, and services.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: But there was one important difference between Brunswick and the other businesses Casey was used to running.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He did not have control.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: When the consortium was formed, Casey's interest was roughly 20%.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Boylan held the largest block of shares.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey would increase his stake as the project grew more desperate, but he never quite gained control.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: I never had control of Brunswick, he would say, for the rest of his life.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: At first, that did not appear to matter.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The most difficult question at the center of the project, how to process the ore, was believed to have been answered.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: A British laboratory had tested the process, the experts said it would work, and so construction began.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: But the material used in the tests was not representative of what would eventually come out of the Brunswick mine.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The smelter was being designed before its processes had been proven on the material it would actually have to handle.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: As the plant was designed and redesigned during construction, its estimated cost rose from $25 million to over $70 million.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Everyone had a reason to continue.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Robichaux had promised Northern voters a smelter.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Boylan had spent years trying to develop his discovery.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The experts had endorsed the metallurgy, and even Casey's construction companies were earning money from the project.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: But Casey kept returning to a basic question.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Would the economics work?
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: By 1963, he was warning that construction had begun too early.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The plant was being redesigned while it was being built.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And he asked Rubichaud to slow the project down until the technical questions were settled.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Otherwise, they were just wasting money.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The Premier, of course, refused.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He had promised the North a smelter.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The province had guaranteed millions of dollars in loans, and the agreements required the project to meet a deadline, delaying construction risks looking like abandonment of the entire development.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey pressed him again, but the answer remained no.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Experts assured both men that the problems could be solved, and Casey eventually backed off.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: At a public ceremony for the project, he stood before the crowd and said that a dream was about to be fulfilled.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Then the smelter opened.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: It could not process the Brunswick mine's output as planned.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: For months, they adjusted, experimented, and spent millions trying to make the plant do the one thing that it was supposed to do.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The mine itself was good.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: There was valuable ore in the ground, and the company could make money by digging it out and selling it to other processors.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: As one senior mining executive later put it, Brunswick could have been a prosperous company if it had never built the smelter.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: By 1967, the company was approaching bankruptcy and needed tens of millions of dollars to survive.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey assembled a rescue plan worth more than $60 million.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Accepting it, however, would have placed control of the project in his hands.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And Robichaux couldn't allow his government to do that.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: They chose Noranda instead.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The Toronto Mining Company agreed to supply the money, pay down the debts, and finish the project.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: In return, it received the one thing KC never possessed at Brunswick, voting control, 51% to be precise.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And I'm sure that number was not lost on KC.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: While KC's money remained inside the company, his influence over it diminished.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The smelter continued to disappoint.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey had acquired New Brunswick's newspaper slowly.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: In 1944, he bought the company that published St. John's two daily papers.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Four years later, he acquired control of the two Moncton Papers.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Newspapers had come up for sale, and he had bought them just as he had bought sawmills, ships, and hardware companies.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: They were businesses that could be improved, connected to others, and protected from outside influence and control.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: A newspaper even fit the closed industrial loop, the vertical integration that Casey had spent his lifetime assembling.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02
