speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: If an attack on the Irving interests was an attack on New Brunswick, he suggested, then Casey had become something larger than a businessman.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: His private interests had become entangled with public interests of an entire province.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey resisted this characterization.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: I'm not sure of your reasoning, he said.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: I think we're kind of grasping at straws here.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He retreated to the narrower point he believed he had been making.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: When New Brunswick prospered, everyone in the province prospered, including him.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The committee returned to the newspapers.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey explained that he regarded them as good businesses.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He had bought them as he bought other companies, partly because he did not want them falling into outside hands.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The chairman asked when concentrated newspaper ownership would begin to trouble him.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey said he would be concerned if one person owned every newspaper in Canada while living somewhere like Toronto.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: A distant owner might not care about the communities those newspapers served.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The committee's lawyer saw an opening.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Would Casey be concerned if one person owned every newspaper in Manitoba or Ontario, just as he owned every English language daily in New Brunswick?
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: That, he said, would depend on the owner, on their motives.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Now, I want to pause here just for two quick beats.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: First, this question is actually more relevant than ever today because journalists' salaries are increasingly subsidized by governments.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: So if you were listening to this and that argument resonated with you that one person shouldn't have so much power, that's the argument that the Irving's critics made, that he didn't need to exercise his power to shape what was covered, how it was covered, and what was omitted.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And this should concern you, as newspapers are meant to oppose political power, no matter who is in charge.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Increasingly, newspapers in the Western world are becoming subsidized by government.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: As their subsidies grow, this same argument is actually taking place.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The very reason the government challenged him was you don't have to exercise that power to have it is the exact same thing happening now, except the person with the power is government.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Second, I don't think this hearing was ever about newspapers.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: It was about putting a successful man in his place.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And there's nothing more Canadian than that.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Okay, let's get back to our story.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: While Ottawa debated what Cayce might do with all that power, Cayce kept doing what he'd always done, building.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: At 70, he announced another $40 million expansion of the St. John Refinery.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: At 71, he opened Canterport, a deepwater terminal where the largest oil tankers could unload beyond the reach of the harbor's tides.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Other men his age were long retired while Casey Irving was planning for the future.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Then, in December 1971, everything arrived all at once.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The federal government charged Casey Irving Limited with criminal offenses under the Combine's Investigation Act.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: After years of investigation, the argument over whether Casey had become too powerful was moving into a courtroom.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: His wife Harriet was ill, her heart was failing, and her doctors advised a warmer climate.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And the tax laws changed.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The federal government was ending its estate and gift taxes.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: A new capital gains tax would apply to increases in asset values from 1972 onward.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Those gains could be taxed at death, even if the assets had never been sold.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: New Brunswick intended to impose succession duties of its own on top of this.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: For Casey, the problem was where his wealth was held.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: His fortune was not sitting in a bank account.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: It was inside refineries, pulp mills, ships, forests, trucking companies, and newspapers, nearly all of which was tied up in private companies controlled by the family.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The taxes, of course, would have to be paid in cash.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: If Casey died while legally a resident in New Brunswick, his estate might have to raise an enormous sum.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: There was no public market where his sons could simply sell a few shares.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: They might have to sell businesses or bring in outside owners to raise money.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: A large tax bill could put the family's control at risk.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The government had finally found a way to dismantle the Irving empire.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: It could leave the family with a tax bill so large that dismantling it was the only way to pay.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey, of course, could not accept this.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: For more than 50 years, he had followed the same rule, keep control.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He had borrowed money but resisted surrendering ownership.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He had poured the profits back into the companies and communities in which they operated and spent decades preparing his sons to inherit them.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He wanted to leave those businesses together, and now death itself could pull them apart.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: His sons, Jim, Arthur, and Jack were in their 40s and had spent most of their adult lives learning the businesses.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Friends were already telling Casey that it was time to step aside.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: But he had never been very good at stepping aside.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: On the other hand, Harriet was ill, the criminal case was advancing, and the new tax rules would take effect on January 1st.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: So the richest man in New Brunswick, and likely the country at that time, decided it would be too expensive to die in Canada.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And so he left.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And he wasn't the only one.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: On December 23, 1971, Casey and Harriet flew to Bermuda.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: His sons remained in St. John to run the companies.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: There was no farewell ceremony or public announcement.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The departure was so sudden that Harriet's knitting remained unfinished at the family home.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The telephone began ringing.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Reporters wanted to know where Casey had gone.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Business people wanted to know whether the rumors were true.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Even the mayor called.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: For three weeks, Casey said nothing.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Then a reporter found him and Casey issued a short statement.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: I'm no longer residing in New Brunswick.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: My sons are carrying on the various businesses.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: As far as anything else goes, I do not choose to discuss the matter further.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: While it sounded like retirement, it wasn't.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey had not sold the companies or abandoned them.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He had simply changed his residence.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: To his critics, the meaning was simple.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The richest man in the province would rather leave than pay his taxes.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: I think Casey saw a different choice.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He had invested every moment and penny he had into building his empire in the province.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He had created industries, employed people, and reinvested all profits into the very province now coming after him.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Staying meant a tax bill for his sons they could not pay off by selling parts of the businesses, not only dismantling his empire, but risking thousands of jobs.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Once he became a resident of Bermuda, he had to count his days carefully.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He could still return to St. John, but now he counted those visits, marking his days in Canada on a calendar.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He wanted no doubt about where he legally resided.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: By January 1974, with so many people fleeing the province, New Brunswick had suspended its succession duties.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey did not move back.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: While he had beaten the tax deadline, the criminal case followed him.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: At trial, the judge found that the newspapers had complete editorial autonomy.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Their circulation had increased, their facilities had improved, and there was no evidence whatsoever that Casey had interfered with their journalism or harmed the public.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He also found the whole thing was motivated for political reasons.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And then he convicted the company anyways.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The judge believed that concentrating so much ownership in one company justified a presumption of harm to the public.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The appeal courts would disagree.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The companies were fined $150,000 and ordered to sell two papers.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Asked whether the experience had discouraged him from buying more, Casey replied, why that would just be like tossing raw meat in front of a hungry dog.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: When the judge died the following year, his family asked Casey to serve as the honorary pallbearer.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He accepted.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And the wrongly convicted man became an honorary pallbearer for the judge who had wrongly convicted him.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The appeal courts overturned the convictions unanimously.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: A monopoly, it ruled, was not automatically a crime.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The government had to prove that Casey's ownership had harmed the public or was likely to do so.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: It had not.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: In 1976, all nine judges of the Supreme Court of Canada agreed.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Altogether, 13 judges had heard the case, 12 had sided with the Irvings.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The court had not declared a concentrated ownership harmless, however.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: They had required the government to prove that it had harmed the public or was likely to.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Ownership alone was not enough.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The government had tried to force the family to sell its newspapers and failed.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: But while Casey fought to keep control in the family, his sons were taking on more of the work he had once insisted on doing himself.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: They were now running the empire.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The public learned that Casey had stepped aside through the signature on a contract.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: In 1972, Irving Oil entered an exploration agreement.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Arthur Irving signed it as chairman, president, and chief executive officer.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: There was no announcement.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: There was no need to brag about it, Arthur later explained.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The brothers divided the empire.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Jim took the forest, mills, and shipyard.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Arthur took the oil business.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Jack took the properties, hardware, and steel.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: They lunched together, argued, and settled disagreements by majority vote.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey claimed he stayed out of their way.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: When I quit, I quit.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: His sons had learned the business from the ground up.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: While much less ferocious than their father, they were every bit as competent.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: What came next surprised everyone.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The sons grew the empire faster than its founder had.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: They acquired complete ownership of Irving Oil, removing its final outside shareholder.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: They brought on another newspaper mill.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The shipyard won the contract to build Canada's new naval frigates, work that became one of the largest shipbuilding programs in the country's history.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The most important inheritance Casey left his sons was not the empire itself, but the habits that had built it.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: A reporter saw those habits in 1989 when three of Canada's richest businessmen picked him up in a green Ford van.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The brothers wore old coats, rubber boots, and beaver-skinned hats.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And they stopped for lunch at an Irving gas station.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Sitting at the table, Arthur pointed to the ketchup.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Heinz, he said.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The other guy doesn't use Heinz.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Then the coffee cream.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: 18%, he said.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The other guy uses 12%.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Then the napkins.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Big napkins.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The other guy uses small ones.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: That, Arthur explained, was the secret.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Better ketchup, richer cream, and better napkins.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: It sounds ridiculous until you remembered that their father had built an oil empire partly by keeping service station washrooms cleaner than anyone else's.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The smallest details matter.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: While the empire had changed hands, the religion was still the same.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey had spent his life fighting anyone who tried to take his money.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He was also giving away more of it than almost anyone knew.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: His generosity followed the same rule as his businesses.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey made the decision.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: If you pressured him, he'd give you as little as possible.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: But if you left him alone, he might give you a lot more than you imagine.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: A fundraiser once cornered him about financing a curling rink.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey agreed to buy one share, just like everyone else.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: On the other hand, sick employees sometimes found themselves aboard an Irving plane bound for a Boston clinic.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Children of longtime workers discovered that Casey had quietly paid their university tuition.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: When representatives of the new university came asking for $25,000, Casey consulted his sons and returned with an offer of half a million.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He refused to discuss his gifts.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He also refused to put his name on his building.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Years later, a group restoring St. John's Capitol Theater approached Arthur Irving.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: They hoped to name it the Casey Irving Theater.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: They want to do what?
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey asked.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Name the theater after you, Arthur explained.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Do they want some money?
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Probably.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Well, give them some money on the understanding that they keep my name off of it.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey wanted money to do something.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He did not need it to tell the people who had done it.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Harriet died in 1976 after 49 years of marriage.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Without her, the man who had always known exactly what to do appeared lost.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: His voice caught when he spoke about her.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: None of what he had accomplished, he began telling people, would have been possible without her.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Age altered almost everything around Casey Irving and almost nothing inside him, the same as his fortune.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Near his 90th birthday, he visited a mill with his son Jim.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: When Jim pulled a long strip of toilet paper from the roll to clean his glasses, Casey watched in alarm.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Jimmy, Jimmy, what are you doing?
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: You're being a bit extravagant, aren't you?
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Jim Irving was 60 years old and ran some of the largest businesses in the country.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He rolled the toilet paper back and used two sheets.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Forbes later estimated Casey's fortune at $8 billion when a reporter told him the figure Casey smiled with a boyish grin.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Is that all?
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: At 91, he had spent six weeks in intensive care in St. John.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: One morning, he telephoned Arthur.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Art, I want to get out.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Arthur started to answer.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Today, Art, get me out of this place.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And a plane was in the air within an hour.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey checked himself out of the hospital and by nightfall, he was back in Bermuda.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He wanted control to the end.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The following December, Casey returned to St. John for Christmas.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He stayed in the apartment above the Irving headquarters at 300 Union Street.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Sixty-seven years earlier, his automobile showroom had stood on the same ground.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He died there on a Sunday morning in December 1992.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He was 93.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: His sons and grandchildren held the companies.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: There was no outside partners left, the succession had worked, and Casey's preferred definition of ownership had finally been achieved across the empire.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: One hundred percent.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The next day, the Telecraft Journal devoted eight pagers to him.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Its obituary ended with the simplest possible description.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey Irving, dead at 93.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He was a builder.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The crowds overflowed the church at his funeral, the prime minister called, the premier attended.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Some of the strongest tributes came from the men who had fought him.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Louis Robichaux said the admiration for Casey had never left him.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: We had our ups and downs, but I never lost my admiration for his courage and determination.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Their rift had never healed.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey, Robichaux explained, had a memory like an elephant.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: They buried him beside Harriet in Bermuda, an ocean away from Bactouche.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The empire remained together for years.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Eventually, it changed shape.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The forest mills and shipyard went one way, the oil company went another.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey had prevented outsiders from breaking his empire apart.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He could not prevent time, family, and competing ambitions from rearranging it.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey was a fierce man who wanted control and almost never backed down.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He could be stubborn, unforgiving, and utterly convinced that his judgment was better than anyone else's.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Those qualities created enemies.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: They also allowed him to keep going when almost anyone else would have quit.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He borrowed when banks doubted him.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He built when larger companies ignored New Brunswick.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He risked his own capital, reinvested the profits, and prepared his sons to carry the businesses forward.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: He gave money away quietly and refused to put his name on the gifts.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: When the province's politicians came to see him as a threat, Casey fought them.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: When its tax laws threatened the ownership of his companies, he left, but left the businesses, the investment, and the jobs in New Brunswick.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The province had helped create Casey Irving.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Then it became afraid of what it had created.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Casey, in turn, came to distrust the government of the place he never stopped considering home.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Still, he kept betting on it.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: People rooted for Casey not because he was always right.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: They rooted for him because he was never halfway committed.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Whatever the project demanded—money, work, reputation—he gave it everything he had.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And part of that wager was still growing at Blackbrook.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: In 1957, 58-year-old Casey had planted spruce seedlings on land where experts said they would not grow.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: One expert even promised to eat his textbooks if they survived.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: By 1986, the program had planted 200 million trees.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: At 87, Casey put the 200 millionth seedling into the ground himself.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The planting continued after his death.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Sixty years after the first seedlings entered the soil, the count passed one billion.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: I wonder if that professor ever ate those pages that he promised.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: In the end, Casey Irving gave New Brunswick his money, his energy, and nearly his entire working life.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The one thing he would never give it was control.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: That refusal had built an empire, and it created enemies.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Eventually, it drove him out of his home.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: It also persuaded a 58-year-old man to plant something he knew he would never live long enough to harvest.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And that is the story of Casey Irving.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Thanks for listening to Outliers.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Give us a follow and I'll see you next week.
